# CollectivIQ launches AI workers for workplace roles  
Wed, 12th Aug 2026 (Yesterday)  
[SEAN MITCHELL Publisher](https://cfotech.news/author/sean-mitchell)  
CollectivIQ has launched Digital Direct Reports, an AI feature that assigns software agents to defined workplace roles. The product is available within the company's platform.  
The Boston-based company said the feature is intended to let organisations deploy AI workers for roles such as project management, executive support, software engineering, recruitment and data work. Unlike general AI assistants, each agent is assigned a specific function and can operate across the business software employees already use.  
Each Digital Direct Report is given a first and last name and configured with tools, permissions and knowledge tied to a particular role. These AI workers can retain context over time, collaborate with one another and carry out tasks within existing workflows, rather than only responding to prompts in a chat window.  
The launch reflects a broader shift in corporate AI use, from question-and-answer tools to software that can manage recurring work. Businesses have been experimenting with AI assistants for drafting text, summarising meetings and retrieving information, but suppliers are increasingly trying to persuade customers to hand over more routine operational tasks to automated systems.
Digital Direct Reports connects with Microsoft 365, Teams, Outlook, OneDrive, Atlassian Jira, Confluence and GitHub. In practice, that means an AI worker assigned to a project team could monitor progress in Jira, coordinate schedules, prepare updates and gather information from company files and communications.  
CollectivIQ also outlined examples for other roles. An executive assistant version could manage calendars, summarise meetings, draft emails and identify priorities. Engineering-focused agents could work with GitHub repositories and support software development processes, while human resources and recruiting agents could organise candidate information and assist with hiring administration.  
The system keeps humans involved in approvals where needed and records activity for audit purposes. Organisations can also monitor how AI workers interact with internal systems and data, a point likely to matter to companies concerned about security, oversight and accountability as they expand AI use.  
According to CollectivIQ, the feature has already been tested within Buyers Edge Platform, the foodservice procurement and technology company whose leadership team also founded CollectivIQ. It also cited an early use case at Mohegan Gaming.  
**Executive view**  
John Davie, Chief Executive Officer of CollectivIQ, set out the company's case for a broader role for AI in office work.
CollectivIQ positions itself as a platform that brings together multiple large language models in one system for business intelligence use. With this release, it is extending that approach from analysis and responses into delegated workplace functions. The main test will be whether companies trust AI workers with ongoing responsibilities inside their own software environments.

# Your Next Coworker Might Be an AI: Inside the Rise of Digital Teammates  
**BOSTON, MA – August 12, 2026** – The line between assistant and colleague in the digital workplace has just been redrawn. Today, Boston-based CollectivIQ announced the launch of Digital Direct Reports (DDRs), a new class of AI designed not merely to answer questions, but to be hired for and hold specific jobs within a company. This move from conversational AI to collaborative AI marks a pivotal moment, forcing us to reconsider the very structure of our teams and the nature of work itself.  
Unlike the general-purpose chatbots that have become ubiquitous, these AI teammates are given names, assigned roles like 'Project Manager' or 'Software Engineer,' and integrated directly into the enterprise systems where work actually happens. The vision is an office where human employees delegate complex, multi-step projects to their digital reports, who then coordinate, execute, and learn from the experience.
## The Dawn of the Digital Colleague  
CollectivIQ's launch moves beyond the now-familiar concept of an AI assistant. Instead of a single, all-knowing oracle, the company envisions teams of specialized AI agents working together. An AI Executive Assistant might manage your calendar and draft emails, while an AI Project Manager monitors Jira boards for risks, and an AI Recruiter sifts through candidate data to streamline hiring. They are designed to own functions, not just complete isolated tasks.  
"As AI becomes part of every business, the next opportunity will go well beyond simple AI chat," said John Davie, CEO of CollectivIQ, in the announcement. "Instead, the next iteration of AI impact will center on putting that intelligence to perform proactive work like a good junior employee." This framing is key; it positions AI as a subordinate to be managed, a resource to be delegated to, fundamentally altering the human-AI interaction model from one of query-and-response to one of management-and-execution.

The company describes its product as an “AI consensus platform” that allows administrators to assign employees access to different classes of AI models according to their roles, departments, business requirements and budgets.
UPDATED 09:00 EDT / JULY 27 2026 · AI · by Paul Gillin · Boston-based startup CollectivIQ Inc. is targeting runaway artificial intelligence costs with a platform intended to give businesses control over how models are used. The company describes its product as an “AI consensus platform” that allows administrators to assign employees access to different classes of AI models according to their roles, departments, business requirements and budgets.
The features address a growing problem for companies that are moving generative AI from small experiments into broader production use. Reasoning models, background processes and autonomous agents can consume tokens without employees or managers having a clear view of the resulting expense. Recent high-profile examples include Uber Technologies Inc. burning through its entire annual AI coding budget in just four months and Swan AI Inc. running up a $113,000 monthly bill for a four-person team. CollectivIQ said its new controls expose usage at both the employee and company levels and allow administrators to restrict background and agentic work.
